name: 3D Production Pipeline
description: Developed an internal 3D production pipeline combining a C/C++ 3D engine with procedural workflows

items.label: Stable real-time performance on lower-end devices

service.headline: Leadership wanted to turn 3D rendering into a real service
body: Until that time, a few renders had been produced here and there, but 3D had never been a central, sellable part of a project. The goal was to make it one, but the challenge was to define what to sell, and how.

benchmark.headline: I benchmarked the agency's core industry and mined past client requests
body: I had to shape a strategy grounded in real demand rather than an assumed persona.
I noticed client asked technical requests like 3D exhibits and virtual galleries or custom brand animations. Those insights helped narrow down the possible services to be provided.

stat.label: Of the agency's clients were in semiconductors
Clients asked for 3D enabled digital experience over the year
Major competitors already provided 3D related services

paths.headline: I proposed 2 solutions: one pragmatic, one ambitious
body: The pragmatic path was a 3D module library: fast to build, easy to scale with procedural tools like Blender's Geometry Nodes, ready for static and animated renders in the short term.

The ambitious path was a web-based 3D engine: a longer-term, secondary priority that matched past client requests like virtual tours and 3D galleries, with real upside if built right. This project was explicitly framed as R&D rather than a near-term commercial deliverable.

focus.headline: 84% of the agency's clients were in semiconductors
body: So that's where the library started. I analyzed the agency's client base and built the model set around that industry, layering in recurring patterns and elements pulled from paid stock libraries to round out a complete ecosystem of models and effects.

flexibility.headline: The library had to offer flexibility & technical accuracy
body: Clients care about details like pin count and component type, so I structured the library atomically, the same logic behind web design systems, keeping every element configurable per client. Procedural systems, from PCB generation to abstract pattern generation, kept every render exclusive and fast to produce.

quote.quote: The PCB shape isn't exactly like our product, also the number of pins is not right either
quote.author: Client

performance.headline: Clients worried existing 3D demos were too heavy
body: Three.js and Babylon.js demos in particular raised concerns about losing part of the audience to performance issues. That fear shaped the core goal: performance over photorealism.
I chose C and WebGPU for the engine's core, for tighter memory control, compiled to WASM for the web.

split.headline: Core and UI were split for performance vs productivity
body: The core had to be optimised for performance, as a result I used a DOD (Data-Oriented Design) approach with an ECS (Entity Component System) architecture to optimize computation speed.
The UI, only used during development, used C++ and an object-oriented approach instead, trading some performance for faster iteration and access to libraries like imGui.

branding.headline: Client didn't see any added value in the renders
body: Early feedback was blunt: clients didn't see why a generic render was worth more than a stock image. I built a guideline to anchor each client's actual branding into the render meaningfully, turning it into something a stock library could never produce.
The approach landed, one of the two pitched clients approved the direction on the spot.

speed.headline: The 3D engine felt slow
body: I hunted the bottlenecks down one by one: batching mesh rendering by pipeline, retuning the core PBR shader, and exposing more control over MSAA and post-fx.
The result: a stable 60fps even on a ten-year-old MacBook Pro on a basic scene with shadow mapping sun light.

stat.label: Speed improvement on ambient occlusion baking
After batch rendering meshes per pipeline

profiling.headline: Bottlenecks had to be tracked
body: To better profile the whole project, runtime debug tools were added such as live render-mode switching (boundbox, wireframe, solid, texture), a per-pass latency profiler, and a logging console were built in.

impact.headline: The library paid for itself. The engine paid in knowledge
body: The 3D module library was reused across multiple projects for key visuals, brand refreshes, and infographics, cutting production time by 4 and driving contract renewals through strong client feedback.
The engine is still in development and currently deprioritized, but it produced WebGPU expertise that's ready to apply with Three.js when the opportunity comes up.

list.headline: Narrow efforts on 1 efficient solution rather than 2
list.challenge: The library saved real time but adoption stayed narrow (3 key visuals and 1 infographic).
list.outcome: I wish to develop a strategy as to increase its adoption and use it as a mean to shape the brand's whole 3D direction.

list.headline: Better assessing technical workload for greater result
list.challenge: The WebGPU engine was correctly framed as R&D from the start, which contained the risk, but I still underestimated the build time versus using existing libraries.
list.outcome: I now reconsider more closely existing solution vs reinventing the wheel in R&D.

list.headline: Scale the solution to make it available for others
list.challenge: I'm still the only designer with the 3D skill to use the library, which caps its reach.
list.outcome: The next step would be exporting pre-rendered assets so the rest of the design team can use it without touching the 3D pipeline.
